questions.q: What does the syntax `[:REPORTS_TO*1..3]` match in a Cypher pattern?
options: A chain of REPORTS_TO relationships, anywhere from 1 to 3 hops long
Any relationship type, ignoring REPORTS_TO entirely
Exactly 1 relationship, with 3 as an unused parameter
Exactly 3 relationships, always
questions.explain: The *min..max syntax tells Cypher to match a chain of that relationship type ranging from the minimum to the maximum number of hops.

questions.q: What does `[:REL*]` with no numbers specified mean?
options: Exactly zero hops
Exactly one hop, identical to a fixed relationship pattern
A fully unbounded variable-length path — any number of hops, which can be expensive on a densely connected graph
A syntax error in Cypher
questions.explain: Leaving off both the min and max makes the path fully unbounded, which the lesson calls out as something to use with real caution on dense graphs.

questions.q: In the query `MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Dana Okafor'})-[:WORKS_WITH*2..2]-(coworker:Person) RETURN DISTINCT coworker.name`, what is being found?
options: People exactly two WORKS_WITH hops from Dana — indirect connections through a shared direct collaborator
Every person in the entire graph, regardless of connection
People directly connected to Dana by one hop
Only Dana herself, returned twice
questions.explain: The *2..2 range matches exactly two hops, surfacing indirect connections rather than direct ones.

questions.q: Why does a variable-length path traversal in Neo4j scale with the number of actual matching paths rather than with total table size?
options: Because Neo4j secretly converts the query into a SQL Server recursive CTE behind the scenes
Because Neo4j caches the entire graph in memory before every query
Because variable-length paths are capped at a fixed number of hops internally
Because a relationship is a stored pointer directly connecting two nodes, so traversal follows real pointers hop by hop instead of recomputing joins against indexes
questions.explain: This is the core architectural reason graphs are efficient at multi-hop traversal — relationships are physical pointers, not values re-joined at query time.

questions.q: What would be the relational-database equivalent of finding everyone reachable within a variable number of hops through a many-to-many relationship table?
options: A CREATE INDEX statement solves this entirely
Nested self-joins or a recursive CTE, whose cost still grows with the width of the table and matching rows at each level
There is no relational equivalent at all, even a slow one
A single simple INNER JOIN with no performance implications
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts this with nested self-joins or recursive CTEs in SQL Server, which don't scale the same way a graph traversal does.
